title: The Afterimage Artist
twist: Hana sees a colour that isn't there at all. The green isn't on the wall or in her eye — it's made by tired red-sensing cells, and it shows up as the opposite colour.
briefing: Hana, 13, spends two minutes carefully filling in a big bright-red heart on a poster for the school fair. When she looks up at the white classroom wall, she sees a ghostly green heart of exactly the same shape. It fades after about twenty seconds.
question: Where did a green heart come from, when nothing green was there?

clues.title: Two minutes of red
clues.text: She stared at the vivid red paint for two whole minutes without looking away. Her eyes were fixed on one spot the whole time.
clues.shows: her red-sensing cells working hard for a long time

clues.title: A green ghost on the wall
clues.text: On the plain white wall she sees a green heart, exactly the shape of the red one. It moves wherever she looks.
clues.shows: a colour appearing that isn't actually there

clues.title: Fades in twenty seconds
clues.text: She blinks a few times and the green heart fades away within about twenty seconds. Her eyes feel completely normal.

visual.unit: green ghost strength, 0 s → 20 s later

clues.title: Her friend tries it
clues.text: Her friend stares at the red heart and sees a green ghost too. Then they try a blue square — and both see a yellow ghost.
clues.shows: it happening to everyone's eyes, always in the opposite colour

hypotheses.text: Some green paint splashed into her eye.
hypotheses.flaw: Paint in the eye wouldn't fade in twenty seconds, and her friend saw the same green ghost without touching any paint.

hypotheses.text: The red-sensing cells in her eyes got tired from staring, so when she looks at white the other colour cells 'win' and her brain sees the opposite colour — green — until the tired cells recover.
There's a faint green stain on the wall.
hypotheses.flaw: The green heart moved wherever she looked, and a blue square gave a yellow ghost — a stain can't follow your eyes or change colour.

hypotheses.text: Her eyes are damaged from staring too hard.
hypotheses.flaw: Damage wouldn't vanish in twenty seconds, and her friend's eyes did exactly the same thing.

prediction.prompt: The longer Hana stares at the vivid red paint — from 0 up to 120 seconds (two minutes) — what happens to how strong the green afterimage is?

second.question: If she stared at bright green paint instead, what colour would the ghost be?

transfer.context: Tomás stares at a bright yellow sticky note on his desk for a minute. When he looks at a blank white page, he sees a bluish square.
options: The page has faint blue ink printed on it.
The cells that sense yellow light tired from staring, so the white page looks like the opposite colour, blue, until they recover.
transfer.retryHint: What did Hana's friend see after staring at a blue square?
transfer.explanation: It's the same trick Hana's eyes played, run in reverse. The cells that respond to yellow light tired from the long stare; on white, the unworn cells win and his brain reads the opposite colour, blue, until they recover.

takeaway: Your eyes have cells for different colours. Stare too long at one colour and those cells tire; then white looks like the opposite colour until they recover. That colour is made inside your eyes and brain.
